["Saint Nicholas Bishop, good holy man,  
will you give something in my little shoe, God will reward you then.  
Give them a purse with bells,  
so I will no longer torment you.  
As long as God wills it,  
I love Saint Nicholas.  

Saint Nicholas, good holy man,  
put on your best robe  
and ride with it to Spain,  
bring apples from Oranges,  
plums from Damascus,  
give the little children something.  

Sinterklaas, that good lord,  
comes back every year,  
with his little horses before his wagon,  
thus Sinterklaas comes driving along.  

3.  
You grew in virtue as the years went by,  
flinging away the sins of youth,  
diligently seeking knowledge,  
you became accomplished in it in a short time.  

4.  
With fasting you tamed your body,  
the flesh troubled with a coarse garment subdued;  
your soul, a temple of the Holy Spirit,  
was attached to God day and night.  

5.  
After you were ordained a priest,  
you further cultivated virtue,  
your body waged a hard war,  
so that it would be more subject to the spirit.  

6.  
You sleep and eat much less than before,  
and your drink was only clear water,  
your clothes were plain but neat,  
the spirit always cared for in prayer.  

7.  
When your parents were both dead,  
you inherited a very great treasure from them,  
which you did not squander foolishly  
or lock up in an iron chest.  

8.  
You generously gave it to the poor,  
for you did not keep it as your own,  
but as the dispenser appointed by the Lord,  
through which this deed of yours is also told:  

9.  
In Patara there was a poor nobleman,  
who with his wife had three beautiful daughters;  
but when they had grown old,  
he could no longer provide for their upkeep.  

10.  
So he gave them advice,  
which was deadly evil for their souls,  
that for a sum of money they would stain their purity  
with dishonor.  

11.  
As soon as Saint Nicholas understood this,  
he went by night to the same house,  
threw in through the window a knotted cloth with gold,  
by which one daughter was helped.  

12.  
Again he returned to the household,  
and once more threw gold through the window;  
which caused the second daughter to be married,  
such great power had this hidden gold.  

13.  
He also provided for the third daughter,  
and one night brought the money into the house,  
through which he saved her body from need  
and her soul from death.  

14.  
O wise and merciful prelate,  
you know our miserable state,  
through which our reckless youth  
is quickly carried away from their innocent virtue.  

15.  
Obtain for us from God a devout disposition,  
that always purely does His will;  
give us the gold of love in our shoe,  
so that we escape the punishment of God's rod.  

Before him, whether money or delicacy,  
the night before Christmas is kept:  
there is found some sugar in it,  
some money, some fruit, some more or less,  
according to what it has previously  
lived according to father's and mother's will:  
for if it has shaved the beast too hard  
and has been too bad,  
Saint Nicholas will put a rod in his shoe  
instead of money.", 'There, the journey is done;
The Prize costs us dearly.
It went terribly;
It was nothing but blood, and fire,
And smoke, and dreadful shouting:
What a guest we became!
But just so you know, the brave sailor
Also took some hits!
The Captain led us constantly,
In the heat of the fight,
We all flew in his footsteps;
Just as the man says.
Everything really went well:
And if it had to be this way,
Not a day were we at sea,
When look, a Brigantine,
Came boldly towards us;
How happy we were then!
Although it gave us full force,
We held firm;
And gave back as well as we could.
The bullets whizzed by;
They beat fiercely on the drum
By them, and on our board.

What did we have standing?
Our rudder was theirs.
We shouted: "Long live the Fatherland,
The Devil take the Brit."
They shouted nothing but: dam you, dam!
Dutch Devils! bless the King.
And I hardly know how it happened
That I sustained a wound,
Somewhere at the side of my neck;
The blood dripped long on my vest:
Well, tin box, how faint I grew!
And Flipmaat got the rest.

He fell dead as a doornail, that good fellow.
Well, that's how it was! See there,
His bravery is known to us,
It troubled us all:
But, come, he died on the bed of honor,
As the proverb goes:
A brave Sailor asks for no more.
Once we all must get out.
But it worries me terribly about his wife;
Who knows how she suffers!
There she sits with a child four or five;
She has lost her husband after all.

We still have many wounded;
But only Flip is dead.
The Brigantine got its share
Of bullets, powder, and scrap.
Then we all boarded,
Like Lions at board;
My wound did not stop me there,
I just kept on.
They then risked one chance,
We became somewhat wiser!
And so we ended that dance:
"Hooray! The ship is Prize."
We were in no good mood;
We received bad news:
How gladly would we have fought
In the hold again over news!
I gave one such a good hit,
He crashed against the deck.
And if mate Hein had not prevented it,
I would have given him more on his face!
What did he have
To curse at a sailor?
Is fighting not free for us too?
Look, I was furious angry.

Then the Captain gave a new order
That no one should harm them:
The man undoubtedly meant well,
Although I regretted it at the time.
But, while I walk up and down,
And fly front and back,
I see a Pea Coat in the crowd,
Who, if I am not mistaken,
Is my old faithful schoolmate.
And it was just right;
I called to him: "Were you there, Kris?
That went well."

"For sure!" he shouted, "now that's good,
The Prize is well deserved;
The Zeeland privateer fought fiercely!"
"But what are you doing here, friend?"
I asked again. "Say, what happened?
You were such a good man;
But if you side with the Englishman,
Then just stay where you are."
"Hey, do you dare ask me that again?"
He shouted; "I am enlightened!
But know, I am a man of honor,
I did nothing against duty."

Then I immediately gave him my hand,
We took a sip together:
And about the dear Fatherland,
He was very busy with.
Yes, yes, it was still the same Cris
As over a year and a day;
That I saw clearly and surely.
I reported to the Captain,
That I had found an old mate here again;
Who showed me a happy face,
And immediately he got something.
The Brigantine is good Prize.
We share that too.
How our flags flutter,
How the Sea roars, how it waves!
How pleasant it is all around here;
What heavenly weather!
How the big drum now rolls
To honor the boatswain!
How well organized and clever it is here!
What a Captain we have!
What good luck we get here!
How clean the air is here!

There I see Vlissingen’s towers already.
Ha! It goes like a flash.
What Women stand on the shore;
You know how Women are.
Curious! well, it can happen,
Everyone waits for their own at home,
Or follows a Neighbor Woman for the gossip.
What noise they make!
They wave us with cloths and hats,
And all are equally happy.
Come, come, that's just how it is...
I see children there too.

They point to the Brigantine,
And hope for much Booty.
Whether we are also welcome in the evening!
Even if it is not completely safe;
That did not say little sand, come, a pirate knows little about that.
It still pains me about Flipmaat,
He was such a good man.
The wife will get her share, that’s true,
And also pulls widow’s money;
But I don’t know, it was such a nice couple:
Who will tell her?

Oh Vlissingen! Renowned since ancient times,
For free Piracy,
Isn’t that cleared up by us?
We will come to you quickly;
But soon go back to Sea,
As soon as it suits us.
And if we bring no Prizes,
Then it goes beyond guess...
Now we fire, to honor the City,
Once more with all the Cannon...
There we get the Salvo back,
As beautiful as it could be had.', "1.

was punished by the Jade Emperor,  
descended underground,  
and looked around the four directions;  
“I have nothing left to do at all.  
Let me weave on the loom, or what else?  
Let me weave on the loom, or what else?  
I have nothing left to do at all.”  

Holding the silver axe, she sharpened it,  
cutting the cinnamon tree that spread eastward.  
She pruned the branches and trimmed the twigs,  
cutting off the middle section,  
and slowly planed it with a silver plane.  
She picked and tied the warp threads tightly,  
and lay down the loom.  
The loom is good,  
but with nothing to do, it’s a serious matter.  

Looking back at the jade railing,  
the jade railing was empty.  
The back legs were lowered,  
and the front legs were raised.  
“What else but to weave on the loom?”  

She caught clouds and hung the shuttle,  
and when she tried the shuttle stick,  
the three brothers were clearly visible.  
When she tried the pressing bar,  
the widower was clearly visible.  

The playing sheep with their hooked eyebrows,  
like the fisherman Kang Tae-gong  
throwing a fishing rod in the Usugang River,  
swaying and waving as if saying, “Hey, hey,”  
playing well.  

The fairy sitting on the plum blossom branch,  
pushing the weaving bat as if  
losing her beloved even at thirty,  
pushing here and there,  
her appearance is pitiful.  

Even the loom’s sticks seem  
bent like the green and yellow dragons,  
swaying and playing well.  

The sound of the damp clay pot,  
made by splitting the jade rabbit,  
and the sounds of the millet pot being struck,  
are charming and neatly composed.  

The sound nailed down firmly—  
the drum called Buk—  
with the blue magpie sitting on its eggs,  
and the white cloud flying through the gap,  
swaying here and there, playing well.  

The grinding shuttle:  
one half here,  
the other half there.  
On the seventh day of the seventh month (Chilseok),  
the cowherd and the weaver girl cross paths.  

The playing sheep are  
the old man’s illness or not,  
trying lying down and sitting up,  
the sound of the “Won-san” song,  
in the morning frost and cold wind,  
sounds like a lone wild goose calling for a mate.  

The naturally curved staff  
keeps going persistently,  
trying pushing and pulling.  

When weaving fine silk,  
fold the silk carefully and bind it.  
Using the silver-headed knife,  
fold the silk and bind it.  
Fold the silk and bind it.  

Boiling sweet potato starch in water,  
lift it slightly,  
put it in the front river,  
wash it in the back river,  
and using grass like jade,  
spread it on the wooden frame.  

“Let’s weave, let’s weave,  
let’s weave your clothes.”  
“What kind of clothes should I weave?”  
“Try weaving raw silk.”  

Holding silver thread in hand,  
sewing blessings with a golden needle,  
she wove your raw silk garment.  
“I have nothing left to do at all.”  

Carefully and neatly folded,  
laid it on a half-moon,  
went outside to the yard,  
and said, “Our groom must be coming.”  

He is coming,  
but is it our groom  
or not?

what’s the matter with the Chilseong bench?”

if it opens and closes, won’t I go through it?

Such is the fate of the four pillars of destiny, so my mind is restless.  
Let me try singing a twisted song:  
The twisted leg is a death sentence,  
Your leg is a single leg,  
At the time of conception, there are three legs.  
The goose caught at conception walks like the male organ;  
They sit one after another.  
Generously placing a gambler’s hand with ease,  
Playing foolishly, there is no way to resist the small songs.  
Hehe, the empty sheep sits on three legs,  
Endless with silver food, the twang of the plucked bow fades,  
Is it the sound of the lone wanderer in Gyeongju?  
The cry of the dove at dawn in the clear sky,  
Crying alone as it goes.  
The crooked tree of faith hangs its neck with worn-out rope,  
Sighs when climbing up and sighs when descending.  
The three-tiered acorn cluster withers after one morning,  
Pitiful is this fate—pulling in the front water and licking in the back water,  
Spoon by spoon, it plays and unravels like the sound of children.  
Let our husband try on a real jin robe,  
I tried searching for the thread of destiny,  
Looking frantically but life, like a matchstick, inevitably departs.  
Trying to find the ear needle,  
The ears appear and then disappear.  
Picked once, picked twice, alas this is the misfortune of heaven and earth.  
It is sealed, it is sealed, the real jin robe is sealed.  
Nothing can be done, nothing can be done, my husband, nothing can be done.  
Waiting for your return in September, beneath the willow,  
The wild chrysanthemums smell sweet, but why do they bloom so late?  
Passersby each time say our gentleman has not come,  
Passersby answer that something has passed, something is lost,  
Coming down the path of the Seven Stars board.  
Hello, sir, is that true?  
Why lie?  
Losing my mind as I chase, turning at a bend,  
The twenty-eight lunar mansions march in step.  
I trusted the three generations, but the funeral time was the beginning of the curse.  
The silk skirt that was worn was the first curse,  
The straw sandals worn on black feet were also the first curse.  
In the prime of youth, unable to help but return,  
Opening the door and answering, the mandarin duck, golden bedding, and the cabinet—  
With whom are you exchanging words? My soul is gray-haired, I am dying.  
This helpless life, helpless,  
Like raw ointment, like prevention of illness.  

When the bucket drops, it falls as one,  
Listening to the cry, it mourns in a single melody.  
A feeling of one energy, one energy—this fate is one energy.  
Though youth turned to white hair, today we part and see,  
Sighs rise and anger wells up, oh, people of the clear sky,  
Hear these words:  
Having lost a head like a mountain in one day,  
Asking the soul a hundred times, it has grown restless,  
Though my body is like this, not knowing the falling flower and freezing dew, the empty sky is being emptied.  
Hello, sir, if you hear this news, please convey it to my lord:  
Why does the goose in the clear sky wander and cry along the streets?  
Thinking of this fate, goose, goose, you too came out—  
Having lost our beloved together, crossing the Han River, this is the fortune of the world.  
Namu Amitabul Gwansembosal (Amitabha Buddha, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva).']

She held a golden silk thread, but there was nowhere to weave.  
She climbed up to the sky, and in the middle of the moon, there was a cassia tree.  
Branches spread out to the east and south alike.  
When placing the main beam in position,  
Willow knots, are you the wood? Wood, is it you, the timber?  
Bent branches were neatly trimmed, and straight woods were carefully shaped.  
Though a pair of weaving looms were made, there was nowhere to weave.  
Looking around the four seas and eight directions, it was empty, truly empty.  
Even on the jade railing there was no place for the loom to be set.  
The loom’s legs are like sheep’s legs; the big sheep’s legs are club-shaped legs.  
They say they don’t sit, but the sitting sheep took a proper seat.  
The sheep caught in the barn are lively and well taken care of,  
Their waists only slightly wrapped.  
Crossing the north, it is like the blue and yellow dragons protecting their eggs,  
They come and go skillfully.  
When the loom is struck like thunder, early in the morning before dawn,  
The sound of axe chopping is sorrowful.  
The pressing board is single, and the edging pad consists of three brothers.  
The wall eyebrow stick is the oldest brother; canes made by ants,  
The weaving sheep who is annoyed raises thousands of armies,  
Snapping its necks restlessly.

['Dear great God, how have You been dishonored,
By unrestrained, human kind,
For Your name is being
Heavily slandered and brought to disgrace because of our sins;
Oh! what greater evil does one see on many ships,
Where evil is eagerly embraced,
And where everyone,
As if a virtue, drags it forward with joy.
What greater evil does one hear being mentioned,
Slandering and cursing, has become very common;
Many want to repay evil with evil,
Or their mouth is full of light songs,
Of lewd talk, and of drunkenness,
And of venomous gossip,
In this wicked attempt,
Everyone seeks the highest ranks.
Much of their talk is full of horror,
Many must hear much lewdness,
Sometimes they mock the prayers,
Yes, they grieve over it when it is done,
For it is too long to be at Prayer for even a small half hour, oh wicked custom!
Where at the revelry,
One could last a whole day.
Brothers, do you not think if you dishonor God the Lord
Like this, that He will also,
(According to your deserts) torment you with punishment,
In the comfortless sad valley of tears,
Where a bitter woe, with gnashing of teeth,
The evil people will strike most severely,
In the hellish kingdom,
Where it will burn eternally.
But this is not said to you all,
As if God’s names are by everyone
Thus godlessly and slanderously with blasphemies
Dishonored and trampled underfoot,
For there are many who greatly dislike this,
And (for the love of God) complain about it
Serving the Lord,
And also uphold His honor.
But this is said to the open,
Worldly servants, who (as if it were a virtue)
With their tongue continually slander the Lord of Hosts,
With pleasure, and joy,
And with shameless cursing, and horrid swearing,
They go about dishonoring Him most grievously,
And whose heart, stubborn and
Does not turn away from this wicked deed.
Yet I pray you all, flee such works,
Take heed to God’s Word,
Keep His Law,
Serve Him as He teaches you in His Churches,
Turn away from evil, and pursue good,
Then God will also protect and guard you,
From the violence of the waves
In your journey,
Storms, and sorrow
Will then not burden you.
If you serve Him thus, and evil comes your way,
Then His mercy will abundantly
Be your help, He will not abandon you,
If you cry to Him in distress,
But He will then hear your brief prayer,
And you shall never be lost,
For God has sworn
This covenant through the mouth of His Prophet.
He will give you comfort and help in your pressure
So that you shall not perish through it,
And over that He will, after this life,
Forgive you all your debts out of grace,
And when you come to die,
You shall obtain the throne of Heaven
Through His good favor!
And His glorious kingdom
You shall also graciously inherit.', 'Yes, flattering little Heart Thief!

At the hour of the Ox, life is born, receiving the Five Elements,  
nurturing all things that grow.

Girls among other peoples;  
Aim for a woman even without dowry,  
Look at women from other villages,

the sharp-tongued mother-in-law stirs her cold water feet.  
"Yesterday you came, my dear daughter-in-law, and today again, my dear daughter-in-law,  
what kind of work is this, coming only for lunch?"  
Hearing that voice, I was so overwhelmed that I couldn’t speak.  
Returning to my room, I tore seven pieces of cloth.  
I used two pieces to make a patchwork pouch, three pieces to make a bag,  
and one piece to make a simple sash, cutting and cutting,  
cutting my hair to look like a monk.  
I was going, but my husband said to go.  
He said he would ride a horse and go to the Seonbun family.  
Wearing half a plain sleeve, I turned around the side door.  
My husband said, "Dear, Shinjung family,  
don’t start any trouble with people.  
Dear, wearing half a plain sleeve,  
turn around the side door."  
At the end of his words, I suddenly grabbed his hand fiercely,  
trembling all over. "What’s wrong with you?  
What’s the matter with you, who usually wears a silk brocade waist bag?  
Why suddenly shave your head, who used to wear a golden hairpin and chop its hair?  
Why wear straw shoes over your worn shoes?  
Let’s go, let’s go back home."  
"I can’t go, I can’t go.  
Your parents' family is good, but I’m different, I have to go."  
Returning home, I asked my mother, "Where did he go?"  
"Since you left, he went away." The words made me so overwhelmed.  
Inside the three-foot coffin, inside the coffin, I cut my neck and died. / Sop'al', 'Behold some new cheerfulness,

instead of money, a rod.", "Hear, sailors all together,

The Farmer must bring the coins,

7. What would the Merchant manage, and also the Shopkeeper,  
How would he sell his wares all too dearly,  
How would he deceive the poor craftsman,  
With wondrous lies as often as he can:  
From where must the Farmers,  
All to the towns bring,  
Butter and Cheese, various grains,  
Of Corn, and of Oats, of Barley and Buckwheat.  

8. The Miller with his Servants would soon perish,  
If he had to be without Grain for three months at once,  
How could he dare to reach so deep into everyone’s sack?  
He would indeed have to fast that the Farmer deprived him,  
The Farmer must supply it,  
So that the Miller can grind,  
The Miller must honor the Farmer, and also the wind,  
The wind and also the Farmers they are the Miller’s friends.  

9. The Brewer would become as skinny as a stick,  
If he could not buy Barley and Malt from the Farmers:  
How could he brew that gentle and fine drink,  
By which many Men and Women so often become satisfied,  
The Brewer and the Baker  
Live off the Farmer’s Acre;  
The Baker would become very poor without the Farmer,  
He would have to sell the Oven and his Peel.  

10. How would young Children grow so quickly,  
If they could not eat the sweet milk porridge?  
How would sick people so soon be healthy again,  
For what they could wish for to the taste of their mouth,  
Fresh Eggs, or a Chicken,  
A Pea, or a Bean;  
A well-roasted Chicken, and also some small bones,  
A Finch, or a Thrush that the Farmer provides them.  

11. How could the old greybeard in the corner of the stove,  
Warm his little feet: he would perish from the cold,  
How could old Women, who are now grown old,  
Live so long in life that they are not helpless,  
And had Buckwheat cakes,  
Where shall we seek them?  
It all comes from the Farmers, the Farmer gathers the wood,  
The Farmer cuts the peat from the moors, quite a lot.

Though I have praised you, it's only in general  
Although you are deserving of praise, although you must be esteemed,

Humility will cling to you,  
Always live in virtue,  
Be thankful to the Creator, and praise Him at this moment,  
And also say every day once Deo gratias."]
